before.content_html:
A Rare Path to Public Life

In ancient Athens and Rome, women were largely excluded from civic and political life. Yet religion offered something different: roles of genuine authority and public visibility that few other spheres of society permitted. A priestess could own property in trust for a deity, lead public ceremonies attended by thousands, and earn the kind of respect usually reserved for men. Understanding these religious roles is essential for evaluating just how restricted—or unexpectedly empowered—women were in the classical world.

Greek Priestesses and Prophetesses

Greek sanctuaries regularly appointed women to serve female deities, and sometimes male ones too. The hiereia (priestess) held a position of real status. The most famous religious role open to a woman in all the ancient world was that of the Pythia, the oracle at Delphi. A woman, believed to be inspired directly by the god Apollo, sat on a tripod above a crack in the earth inside the inner sanctuary of the Temple of Apollo. Suppliants from across the Greek world — individuals, cities and kings — paid substantial fees to consult her, and her pronouncements could shape military campaigns and political decisions. The power she wielded, though in the name of a god, was genuinely extraordinary.

The literary source Plutarch, writing in his essay On the Oracles at Delphi, describes the process in some detail. A suppliant would purify himself, offer a goat sacrifice, pay the consultation fee, and then put his question to the male priests who passed it on to the Pythia in her inner chamber. Her response, often ambiguous, was delivered in prose or verse and interpreted by the priests. Plutarch was writing in the Roman period, long after the height of the oracle’s influence, but his account helps us picture how the consultation worked. The Pythia herself remained anonymous — we know no individual Pythia by name from the classical period — which tells us something important: her power came from the god, not from her personal identity.

Key Fact

The Pythia was the prophetess of Apollo at Delphi. She was a woman (usually an older woman taken from ordinary life) who delivered divine pronouncements to suppliants from across the Greek world. Her role gave women unparalleled spiritual authority in the Greek world.

Women’s Roles in Greek Festivals

Several major Athenian festivals required female participants. The Thesmophoria was one of the most widespread festivals in the Greek world, celebrated by citizen women across Athens and many other city-states. For five days each autumn (the Athenian Thesmophoria lasted five days in Attica, though only three days in much of the rest of the Greek world), citizen women left their households, set up camps near a sanctuary, and performed secret rites connected to the fertility of the earth and the myth of Persephone’s descent to the underworld. Men were completely excluded. The festival required women to take on significant organisational roles: the wealthiest women funded the ritual costs, and others carried out the ceremonial acts. The Thesmophoria demonstrates that certain religious spaces belonged entirely to women.

The Great Panathenaia was a very different festival. Here women participated prominently alongside men in a great civic procession along the Sacred Way to the Acropolis. The Parthenon Frieze — a continuous carved marble relief running around all four sides of the outer wall of the temple, now largely in the British Museum — appears to depict elements of the Panathenaic procession. Women and girls are carved in the frieze presenting offerings and walking in stately procession. Whether the frieze shows mortals or heroised figures is debated by scholars, but it places women at the visual and religious heart of the city’s most important civic celebration.

In ancient Athens, women played the central role in preparing the bodies of the dead and leading lamentation. The ritual of prothesis (laying out the corpse) was performed entirely by women. They washed the body, anointed it with oil, wrapped it in grave clothes, and led the communal mourning. Female mourning was considered both a religious duty and an expression of proper piety. However, Athenian law codes in the fifth century BC attempted to restrict female lamentation in public as being too emotionally excessive. The fact that legislation tried to curb it suggests how powerful and public women’s religious mourning actually was.

Roman Priestesses: The Vestal Virgins

Rome’s most prominent female religious institution was the college of Vestal Virgins. There were six Vestals at any time, each serving for thirty years: ten years of training, ten years of active service, and ten years of teaching new initiates. They were recruited between the ages of six and ten from respectable Roman families. Their central duty was to tend the sacred flame of Vesta in her circular temple in the Roman Forum. The flame represented Rome’s vitality; if it went out, disaster for the city was feared.

The legal position of the Vestal Virgins was extraordinary for Roman women. Normally, a Roman woman was under the legal authority of a male guardian (paterfamilias or tutor). The Vestals were freed from this authority: they could make wills, own property, give testimony in court without taking an oath, and travel through the city in a special carriage. They were accorded seats of honour at public games. If a Vestal passed a condemned criminal on the way to execution, he was automatically pardoned. This combination of purity requirements with extraordinary legal privilege marks the Vestals as unique in the Roman world. In exchange, the requirement of chastity was absolute: a Vestal found guilty of breaking her vow was buried alive in a small underground chamber sealed with earth.

Key Fact

The Vestal Virgins held unique legal privileges: they were freed from the authority of a male guardian, could make wills, own property, and give testimony in court. A condemned man they passed received an automatic pardon. The penalty for breaking their vow of chastity was to be buried alive.

Other Roman Religious Roles for Women

Alongside the Vestals, Rome had other female priestly roles. The Flaminica Dialis was the wife of Rome’s high priest of Jupiter. She was not simply a supporting spouse: her own purity and ritual behaviour were as strictly regulated as her husband’s, and she shared the burden of numerous taboos. Roman women also participated in the worship of the Bona Dea (Good Goddess), whose annual December rite was conducted entirely by women in the house of a senior magistrate. Men were forbidden from even knowing the details of the ceremony. Cicero’s speeches describe the scandal caused by Publius Clodius Pulcher, who disguised himself as a woman to infiltrate the ceremony in 62 BC.

Rome also had a tradition of the Sibyl, a prophetess whose oracular books were consulted by the Roman Senate in times of crisis. The most famous was the Cumaean Sibyl near Naples. These prophetesses, like the Pythia, exercised their authority through divine inspiration rather than civic office — but the effect was the same: a woman whose words could redirect the course of Roman policy.

Both Greek and Roman religion gave women formal roles that granted public visibility and status unmatched in other areas of life. Greek priestesses served a wide range of deities; Roman religion created a more structured institution in the Vestals. Both cultures had female prophetesses (Pythia / Sibyl) whose authority came from divine inspiration. A key difference is that the Vestals also had legal privileges that extended well beyond the religious sphere, suggesting Rome went further in recognising women’s religious service with tangible civic rewards. In Greece, the Pythia’s power remained strictly religious and her personal identity was submerged in the god’s. The material source, the Parthenon Frieze, shows Greek women in a communal, ordered procession; the round Temple of Vesta in the Roman Forum, with its sacred flame maintained only by women, makes a very different visual statement about female religious authority as the beating heart of the Roman state itself.

practice_questions.text: Name the prophetess who delivered Apollo's oracle at Delphi.
Describe the role and duties of the Vestal Virgins at Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: they tended the sacred flame of Vesta in her temple in the Roman Forum; they served for thirty years (ten training, ten active, ten teaching); they were recruited between the ages of six and ten from good families; they were freed from the authority of a male guardian; they could make wills and own property; a Vestal found guilty of breaking her vow of chastity was buried alive.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which paraphrases a description of the Thesmophoria festival:

'For five days each autumn, the women of Athens left their homes and set up camps near a sanctuary. No man was permitted to enter. The women who could afford it paid for the animals to be sacrificed; others carried out the sacred rites connected with the earth and with the story of Persephone. The festival had to be organised and funded by the women themselves.'

What does this passage reveal about the religious roles available to Athenian women? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A thorough analysis that uses multiple specific details from the passage (e.g. the exclusion of men, the women's organisational and funding roles, the connection to Persephone's myth) and links them to the broader significance of the Thesmophoria as evidence that women had real religious agency and a sacred sphere entirely their own. Draws a supported judgement, perhaps noting the paradox of public religious authority alongside domestic confinement.
Secure: Uses at least two details from the passage and explains what each reveals about women's religious roles. Makes a clear point about what this shows, such as that women could exercise genuine authority and initiative in a religious context.
Developing: Identifies one or two details from the passage and makes a basic observation about women's religious life, but the explanation of significance is limited or undeveloped.
Emerging: Mentions the passage in a general way without specific detail or explains it very briefly without engaging with significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the role of the Pythia was significant for our understanding of the status of women in the ancient Greek world.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying who the Pythia was (the prophetess of Apollo at Delphi). 1 mark for explaining what made her role significant (she influenced political decisions and military campaigns; rulers and city-states consulted her). 1 mark for contextualising this against the normal position of women (Athenian women were typically confined to the home and excluded from public life). 1 mark for a supporting detail (e.g. her identity was submerged in the god, suggesting her authority came from divine inspiration rather than personal status; she was drawn from ordinary women).

practice_questions.text: How far do the religious roles of women in Greece and Rome suggest that women had real power in the ancient world? Use a range of named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, well-structured argument that engages with the key tension: religious roles gave women real authority and public visibility, but this power was bounded, conditional, and defined by purity. Uses named sources from both cultures (Pythia, Thesmophoria, Parthenon Frieze for Greece; Vestal Virgins, Bona Dea rites, Temple of Vesta, Flaminica Dialis for Rome). Compares the two cultures fairly, noting that the Vestals' legal privileges went beyond Greece in giving women tangible civic rights. Reaches a supported judgement: religion gave women genuine power in specific, defined spheres, but this was not the same as equality with men.
Secure: Discusses examples from both cultures with relevant source references and makes a clear argument about the degree of power women held. Sustains an explanation throughout and offers a conclusion, even if not fully nuanced.
Developing: Covers some relevant material from one or both cultures but the argument is uneven. Sources may be named but not fully analysed. The conclusion may be asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: Makes general points about women and religion, possibly listing some roles without explaining their significance or using named sources consistently.

practice_questions.text: How similar were the religious roles available to women in Greece and Rome? Give at least two examples from each culture in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced comparison that identifies both similarities (both cultures had formal female priesthoods, both had female prophetesses whose words shaped state decisions, both had women-only sacred rites) and genuine differences (Vestals had legal privileges beyond the religious sphere; Greek ritual mourning and the Thesmophoria gave women control over important communal rites). Uses named examples from each culture (Pythia, hiereia, Thesmophoria for Greece; Vestal Virgins, Bona Dea, Sibyls, Flaminica Dialis for Rome). Reaches a supported conclusion.
Secure: Gives two clear examples from each culture, identifies at least one similarity and one difference, and supports with named evidence.
Developing: Gives examples from both cultures but the comparison is limited; similarities or differences may be implied rather than stated directly.
Emerging: Covers one culture in more detail than the other, or lists roles without comparing them.

glossary_terms.definition: A woman appointed to perform rituals on behalf of a deity, managing a temple's worship and rites.
The Greek term for a priestess, a woman appointed to serve a particular deity and carry out cult activities.
The prophetess at Delphi who sat on a tripod over a chasm and delivered the pronouncements of Apollo.

A women-only fertility festival held in Athens and across the Greek world in honour of Demeter and Persephone, from which men were excluded. In Athens (Attica) the festival lasted five days; elsewhere in the Greek world it typically lasted three days.
A great civic and religious festival held at Athens every four years in honour of Athena, featuring a procession, contests, and the presentation of a new robe to the goddess.
The Greek ritual laying out of a corpse for mourning, carried out by the women of the household before the funeral procession.
Six women at Rome who served the goddess Vesta by maintaining the sacred flame and received extraordinary legal privileges in return for a thirty-year vow of chastity.
The wife of the Flamen Dialis (high priest of Jupiter at Rome), who shared in her husband's religious duties and was subject to her own strict ritual regulations.
A Roman goddess of good women, worshipped exclusively by women in rites from which men were strictly excluded.
A female prophet in the Roman world; the Cumaean Sibyl's oracular books were consulted by the Roman Senate in times of national crisis.

before.content_html:
Excluded from the Assembly

In classical Athens, political decisions were made by the Ekklesia, the citizen assembly. Any adult male citizen could attend, speak, and vote. Women, slaves, and foreigners were entirely excluded. This was not an oversight: it was a deliberate feature of Athenian democratic ideology, which linked political participation to the qualities of a citizen warrior. Since women did not fight, they were not citizens in the full sense, and they had no voice in the governance of the city that their labour sustained. The philosopher Aristotle, writing in the late fourth century BC, argued that women were naturally suited to the domestic sphere and that their reason was less authoritative than men’s — a view that informed, and was reinforced by, their exclusion from political life.

Aristophanes and the Comic Inversion

The Athenian playwright Aristophanes wrote a comedy called the Assemblywomen (performed around 391 BC), in which a group of Athenian women, led by the resourceful Praxagora, disguise themselves as men, infiltrate the assembly, and pass a law giving women control of the city. The play is prescribed reading for this topic. In the opening section (lines 1–240), we see Praxagora rehearsing her fellow women in how to adopt male mannerisms and speak like citizens. The comedy works precisely because the premise is absurd to an Athenian audience: women running the city is funny because it inverts the natural order entirely. Yet the play is also a pointed satire on the failures of male-run democracy. Aristophanes is not seriously advocating for women’s equality; he is using the device of female rule to mock the incompetence of real Athenian politicians.

The literary source is valuable as evidence precisely for what it assumes: the audience’s automatic understanding that women in politics is ridiculous. That shared assumption tells us a great deal about Athenian cultural attitudes. It also raises questions for students of the ancient world: does the fact that a male author imagined women as capable leaders (however comically) suggest some underlying anxiety about gender and power?

Key Fact

Aristophanes’ Assemblywomen (c.391 BC) depicts women disguising themselves as men to take control of the Athenian assembly. The comedy is only funny if the audience finds women in politics inherently absurd — making it a key piece of evidence for Athenian attitudes towards female political participation.

The Trial of Agnodice

The story of Agnodice is told by the Roman author Hyginus (in his Fabulae) and serves as a significant prescriptive source for this topic. According to the story, Athenian women were suffering from lack of medical care because they were too embarrassed to be treated by male doctors. Agnodice disguised herself as a man, studied medicine, and began practising. When she was accused of seducing female patients, she revealed her sex in court. She was then prosecuted for practising medicine while female — because Athenian law apparently forbade women from doing so. Her female patients rallied to her defence, and the law was changed to allow women to practise medicine for women. The story is almost certainly a legend rather than a historical fact, but it is important evidence for ancient ideas about what women were and were not permitted to do professionally, and for the idea that male-authored narratives could occasionally present women as agents of change.

The seclusion of respectable Athenian women did not mean they had no influence at all. As household managers, wealthy women oversaw budgets, supervised slaves, and made practical decisions that kept the oikos (household economy) functioning. The best-known Athenian woman who challenged these boundaries is Aspasia, the companion of Pericles. Ancient authors — including the hostile comic poets and the philosopher Plato — credited Aspasia with influencing Pericles’ political speeches and even with teaching rhetoric. Because she was not an Athenian citizen (she was from Miletus), she was not subject to the same rules of seclusion, and she reportedly held intellectual conversations with prominent men. Plutarch’s Life of Pericles (chapter 24), a prescribed source, notes that she was prosecuted on charges of impiety and corrupting Athenian women — charges that suggest powerful men felt threatened by her influence.

Women and Roman Politics

The Roman Senate was, like the Athenian assembly, an exclusively male body. Roman women could not vote in the popular assemblies, stand for magistracies, or sit in the Senate. Yet Roman women — particularly those of the aristocracy — had more daily freedom of movement than their Athenian counterparts. They attended dinner parties alongside their husbands, visited temples and public spaces, and were visible in the life of the city in a way that respectable Athenian women were not.

The historian Livy records a remarkable episode: the repeal of the Oppian Law. In 195 BC, groups of Roman women gathered in public and approached male citizens to lobby for the repeal of this wartime sumptuary law. The conservative senator Cato the Elder argued fiercely against repeal, insisting that women needed to be controlled and that their public lobbying was an affront to male authority. He lost. The women’s campaign was successful. Livy presents the episode with some ambivalence — he clearly shares some of Cato’s discomfort about female public action — but the bare fact of the story is that Roman women engaged in collective political action and succeeded.

Key Fact

In 195 BC, Roman women publicly lobbied for the repeal of the Oppian Law, a sumptuary restriction imposed during wartime. Despite Cato the Elder’s fierce opposition, the law was repealed. This demonstrates that Roman women could exercise real collective influence in the political sphere, even though they held no formal political rights.

Sempronia and Political Conspiracy

The historian Sallust, in The Conspiracy of Catiline (chapters 24–25), paints a vivid portrait of Sempronia, an aristocratic woman of remarkable education and talent who was allegedly involved in Catiline’s conspiracy to overthrow the Roman Republic in 63 BC. Sallust describes her as literate in both Greek and Latin, skilled in music and dance, witty in conversation, and possessed of great personal charm. He also accuses her of shamelessness and recklessness, suggesting she craved excitement and excitement made her dangerous. Whether or not Sempronia was genuinely involved in the conspiracy is unclear, but Sallust’s account tells us much about Roman anxiety surrounding educated, independently minded women. Her intelligence and social access, the very qualities that made her admirable in a man, are presented as making her threatening in a woman.

Almost every literary source we have for women in the ancient world was written by men. This matters enormously. When Sallust describes Sempronia’s intelligence alongside her alleged immorality, he is not writing a neutral biography; he is constructing a type: the dangerously clever woman. When Aristophanes puts women in the assembly and makes them figures of comedy, he is not reporting facts but deploying cultural anxieties. Even the sympathetic sources, such as the Laudatio Turiae (a funeral inscription praising a Roman wife for her loyalty during the civil wars), are composed by husbands who celebrate what they valued in women — loyalty, chastity, self-sacrifice — rather than what women valued in themselves. Material sources such as the Parthenon Frieze or the Hegeso Stele can provide a counter-balance by showing women in their own spaces and roles, but they too were commissioned or carved by others. The honest approach is to acknowledge the bias and use it as evidence itself.

Power behind the Throne

The Roman imperial system, which replaced the Republic in 27 BC, created new possibilities for powerful women. An emperor’s wife, mother, or sister lived at the heart of power, had daily access to the most important man in the world, and could influence appointments, policies, and the fate of rivals. The Roman Senate remained exclusively male, but the imperial household was not governed by the same formal rules, and women who knew how to operate within it could be genuinely formidable. Ancient sources — almost all male, almost all hostile — were simultaneously fascinated and alarmed by these women, producing portraits that blend genuine observation with exaggeration and moral condemnation.

Livia: The Perfect Empress

Livia Drusilla was the wife of Rome’s first emperor, Augustus, whom she married in 38 BC. She remained his wife until his death in AD 14 — a period of over fifty years. During the Augustan age she became a public symbol of Roman wifely virtue: chaste, dignified, devoted to her husband and household. Augustus, who was promoting a moral reform programme for Rome, projected Livia as the model Roman matrona. She was depicted in sculpture as serene and modest. The Ara Pacis (Altar of Peace), a great carved marble monument commissioned by the Senate in 13 BC to celebrate Augustus’s return from campaigns in Spain and Gaul, shows Livia in the sacrificial procession alongside Augustus, her children, and senior figures of the state. She is depicted veiled (a sign of ritual purity) and takes her place as a central figure in the Augustan dynasty’s self-presentation.

Yet Livia’s influence went far beyond the ceremonial. Ancient sources, including the historian Tacitus and the biographer Suetonius, hint that she managed significant patronage networks, interceded with Augustus on behalf of petitioners, and exerted influence over matters of succession. After Augustus’s death she received unprecedented honours: the Senate granted her the title “Julia Augusta” and she was eventually deified (made a goddess) under the emperor Claudius in AD 42. The Laudatio Turiae, a Roman funerary inscription (probably dating to the late first century BC and perhaps connected to the civil-war period), praises a Roman wife in similar terms to Livia — loyalty, endurance, and selfless support for her husband — suggesting that Livia represented one ideal end of a spectrum of Roman female virtue that was genuinely valued, not simply invented for propaganda.

Key Fact

Livia, wife of Augustus, was presented as the model Roman matrona: chaste, dignified and devoted. The Ara Pacis depicts her in the dynastic procession, veiled as a sign of purity. After Augustus’s death she was granted the title “Julia Augusta” and was eventually deified under Claudius.

Agrippina the Younger: Power and Danger

Agrippina the Younger represents a more alarming figure in Roman historical memory. As the mother of the emperor Nero and wife of the emperor Claudius, she occupied a uniquely powerful position in mid-first century AD Rome. The historian Tacitus, in his Annals, portrays her as relentlessly ambitious — pursuing power through a series of strategic marriages, allegedly poisoning her husband Claudius to secure Nero’s succession, and then attempting to dominate her son’s reign. Tacitus describes her appearing in public seated on a dais alongside Nero at official ceremonies, receiving foreign ambassadors, and being acclaimed on coins alongside the emperor as a co-regent figure.

Roman coins from the early years of Nero’s reign (AD 54–55) show Agrippina’s head on the obverse (front) of the coin alongside her son, or even placed in front of his head, implying her precedence. This is a material source of great significance: official state coinage is one of the most authoritative forms of public communication in the Roman world, and depicting a woman in this position is extraordinary. Nero eventually had his mother murdered in AD 59, and after her death the hostile portrait in the literary sources hardened. Tacitus’s account must be read sceptically, since it was written well after the events and draws on hostile senatorial tradition.

The portraits of Livia and Agrippina in sources such as Tacitus and Suetonius are deeply shaped by senatorial ideology: powerful women who operated beyond their proper sphere were inherently suspect. Livia is praised where she conformed to the matrona ideal; Agrippina is condemned for the same ambition that would have been admired in a male politician. The material sources — coins showing Agrippina and Nero; the Ara Pacis showing Livia in the dynastic procession — cannot lie in the same way as literary texts, since they were produced for public display. But they too were constructed images: the Ara Pacis was official Augustan propaganda, not a neutral record. Using both literary and material sources together, and asking what each was designed to communicate, gives a more complete picture than either alone.

Cleopatra VII: Rome’s Most Feared Foreign Queen

Cleopatra VII was not a Roman woman, but Rome’s obsession with her makes her essential for this topic. As queen of Egypt she was an independent sovereign ruler with a large army, great wealth, and strategic control of Egypt’s grain supply, on which Rome depended. She forged a political and personal alliance with Julius Caesar after his arrival in Egypt in 48 BC, and later with his successor Mark Antony. The Roman poet Horace, writing after her defeat, calls her a deadly monster who corrupted Roman men with her un-Roman luxury and ambition. Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 8, lines 671–713) depicts the battle of Actium (31 BC) on the shield of Aeneas, where Cleopatra appears as a shameful eastern queen surrounded by monster-gods, opposed by the orderly Roman gods championing Octavian.

In 31 BC Octavian (later Augustus) defeated the combined forces of Antony and Cleopatra at the naval battle of Actium, off the western coast of Greece. Both Antony and Cleopatra subsequently took their own lives, and Egypt became a Roman province. The official Roman interpretation of the war was not a civil conflict between Roman generals, but a war against a foreign queen who had bewitched a Roman man and threatened to move the capital of the world from Rome to Alexandria. By framing Cleopatra as a foreign threat, Octavian could present his victory as the defence of Rome against an alien, feminised East — a narrative that shaped how Cleopatra was remembered for centuries.

Key Fact

Cleopatra was presented in Roman sources as a dangerous foreign queen who had seduced Roman generals away from their Roman values. Virgil’s Aeneid and Horace’s poetry treat her as a moral threat; the shield of Aeneas in Aeneid Book 8 depicts the battle of Actium with Cleopatra on the side of monstrous foreign gods. Her defeat in 31 BC allowed Octavian to present himself as the saviour of Roman tradition.

There is a recurring pattern in how Roman culture handled powerful women: it idealised women who exercised power invisibly (Livia as the perfect wife behind the scenes), feared women who sought visible political power (Agrippina appearing in public as co-ruler), and demonised foreign women who wielded power on their own terms (Cleopatra as eastern monster-queen). Each figure is a mirror held up to Roman anxieties about gender, power, and what it meant to be Roman. The material sources — the Ara Pacis, the coins of Agrippina, the funerary stele tradition across both cultures — remind us that behind the literary constructions were real women whose lives shaped the course of ancient history.

Reversing the Natural Order

Both the Greeks and the Romans showed a persistent fascination with the figure of the warrior woman: a female who took up arms, stepped onto the battlefield, and excelled in the role that ancient culture most exclusively assigned to men. These figures appeared in myth, in epic poetry, and on the walls of public buildings. They were rarely celebrated without ambivalence. A woman who fought was, by definition, doing something she was not supposed to do — and ancient sources show both admiration for her courage and relief when the social order was restored. Studying warrior women in the ancient world reveals as much about the boundaries imposed on real women as it does about the warriors themselves.

The Amazons in Greek Myth and Art

The Amazons were a mythological nation of female warriors, said to live somewhere on the fringes of the known world — in early sources near the Black Sea, later in Libya or other remote regions. Greek myth stressed what made them different from ordinary women: they allegedly cut off one breast to improve their aim with a bow (the name “Amazon” was popularly but incorrectly derived from “without breast” in Greek); they rejected men except for the purpose of reproduction; they chose to fight rather than to weave.

The Amazonomachy (battle against the Amazons) became one of the most popular subjects in Greek public art precisely because it stood for something: the victory of Greek order over barbarism, of civilised men over these dangerous, inverted women. The Bassae Frieze (now in the British Museum) is one of the prescribed visual sources for this subject. This continuous marble frieze originally decorated the interior of the temple of Apollo at Bassae in Arcadia, constructed in the fifth century BC. The frieze, carved in high relief, depicts two battles side by side: on one set of slabs, Lapiths fight Centaurs (the Lapith Centauromachy — the battle at the wedding feast of Peirithoos); on another, Greeks fight Amazons (the Amazonomachy). In both battles, the Greeks are depicted as the forces of order triumphing over chaos, whether that chaos takes the form of half-human monsters or warrior women who have stepped outside their proper role.

Key Fact

The Bassae Frieze is a marble relief from the interior of the Temple of Apollo at Bassae (Arcadia), dating to the fifth century BC, now in the British Museum. It depicts two battles: the Centauromachy (Lapiths versus Centaurs — the battle at the wedding feast of Peirithoos) and the Amazonomachy (Greeks versus Amazons). Both battles symbolise the triumph of Greek civilised order over savage disorder.

Penthesilea: the Amazon Queen at Troy

Penthesilea was the most celebrated individual Amazon: the queen who led her warriors to Troy to fight for the Trojans against the Greeks. Her story does not appear in the prescribed books of Homer’s Iliad, but it was well known in antiquity from other sources, and it was depicted on Greek vases. According to the myth, Penthesilea fought with great courage before being killed by Achilles. At the moment of her death Achilles is said to have fallen in love with her — a paradox that ancient artists found compelling. A famous red-figure cup attributed to the Penthesilea Painter (c. 460 BC) shows Achilles driving his spear into Penthesilea’s throat at the very moment their eyes meet, making the scene simultaneously an act of violence and a moment of recognition between equals.

What does Penthesilea’s death tell us about Greek attitudes to the warrior woman? The pattern is revealing: Penthesilea is given heroic qualities but is ultimately killed by the greatest Greek hero. The Amazon challenge is real but it is contained. The Amazonomachy always ends with the Greeks winning. The warrior woman is admired for her courage but the proper order is restored: men on top, women in their place. This pattern appears throughout Greek culture, from the Bassae Frieze to the metopes of the Parthenon (which also depicted an Amazonomachy on the west side of the temple) to the great mythological battles on Attic vases.

Modern archaeology has found evidence in the steppes of Central Asia (modern Ukraine, Russia, and Kazakhstan) of women buried with weapons, horses, and armour alongside male warriors in nomadic burial mounds (kurgans) dating from around the fifth to the third centuries BC. Some scholars argue these are the historical reality behind the Amazon myth — Greek travellers and traders heard stories of Scythian or Sarmatian women who rode and fought, and converted these into a mythological nation. The ancient Greek historian Herodotus describes the Sauromatae as descended from Amazons and Scythians, and notes that their women rode and hunted. This does not prove that the Amazons of Greek myth were historical, but it does suggest Greek culture was aware that some women in the world beyond Greece did things that Greek women did not.

Camilla in Virgil’s Aeneid

The Roman answer to the Amazon tradition is Camilla, the warrior maiden who appears in Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 11, lines 532–835, a prescribed source). Camilla leads a band of female warriors who fight alongside Turnus against Aeneas and the Trojans. She is described in heroic terms: fast enough that she could run across a field of grain without bending a single stalk, and fierce in battle, equal to the best male warriors on the field. Her dedication to the virgin goddess Diana (the equivalent of the Greek Artemis) marks her as having chosen a life outside the normal female role of wife and mother.

Virgil’s portrayal of Camilla is genuinely admiring: she is brave, skilled, and noble, and she dies heroically. Yet Virgil also provides a cause for her downfall that is significant. She becomes distracted by the sight of a Trojan warrior wearing dazzlingly beautiful armour and gold, and in her desire to strip it from him she breaks off from the battle and is killed from behind. Some ancient and modern readers see this as a gendered comment: Camilla falters because she is distracted by beautiful things, a characteristically “feminine” weakness. Others see it simply as the standard Homeric device of a hero being killed at the moment of pride (hubris). The ambiguity is part of what makes Camilla such a rich figure for analysis.

Key Fact

Camilla is a warrior maiden in Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 11), dedicated to Diana. She fights with heroic skill but is killed when she becomes distracted by a warrior’s beautiful armour. Her fate can be read as restoring conventional order: the woman warrior’s excellence is acknowledged but her downfall reaffirms that the battlefield ultimately belongs to men.

Both Greek and Roman cultures produced warrior women who were admirable but ultimately defeated, and both used the warrior woman to explore the boundaries of acceptable female behaviour. The Amazons in Greek art (Bassae Frieze, Parthenon metopes) are usually foreign or mythological: they are killed by Greek heroes, restoring order. Camilla in Virgil is fighting on the wrong side (against the proto-Roman Aeneas) and is killed by a named Roman soldier. In both traditions, the pattern is the same: excellence acknowledged, death as restoration of order, and a male hero as the agent of that restoration. The key difference is in tone: Greek Amazonomachy tends to be triumphalist, emphasising the victory of civilisation; Virgil’s portrait of Camilla is more elegiac, mourning what is lost when such a heroic figure is cut down. The Bassae Frieze is a public, civic monument designed to celebrate Greek victory; the Aeneid is an epic poem that can afford more nuance.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Bassae Frieze as a prescribed visual source.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: it is a marble relief frieze; it originally decorated the interior of the Temple of Apollo at Bassae in Arcadia; it is now in the British Museum; it depicts two battles side by side — the Centauromachy (Lapiths versus Centaurs at the wedding of Peirithoos) and the Amazonomachy (Greeks versus Amazons); both battles symbolise Greek order triumphing over barbarism and chaos.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which paraphrases part of Virgil's Aeneid Book 11 (lines 760–800) describing Camilla's final moments:

'Camilla had been laying about her fiercely all morning, killing Trojans without hesitation. Then she noticed a Trojan priest wearing gleaming golden armour set with bronze. She forgot herself entirely and turned from the battle to pursue him, wanting that armour for herself. She did not see Arruns stalking her until his spear struck her from behind. She fell from her horse, dying, and as the life left her she sent a last message to her loyal companion Acca.'

What does this passage suggest about Virgil's attitude towards female warriors? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive analysis using multiple details from the passage (Camilla's prowess in battle acknowledged — 'laying about her fiercely'; her distraction by beautiful armour as the cause of her downfall; the pathos of her dying message to Acca; the fact that she is killed from behind, not in fair combat). Engages with the ambivalence in Virgil's presentation: he admires Camilla but her distraction by the golden armour could be read as a specifically gendered weakness, or as standard epic hubris. Connects to broader argument about how warrior women in ancient literature are ultimately defeated to restore conventional order. Reaches a supported judgement.
Secure: Uses at least two details from the passage and explains what they suggest about Virgil's attitude. Makes a clear point about the mixture of admiration and a reassertion of conventional order.
Developing: Identifies one or two details and makes a basic observation, but the analysis of Virgil's attitude is limited or asserted without development.
Emerging: Paraphrases the passage or makes only general observations about warrior women.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Amazonomachy on the Bassae Frieze reflects Greek attitudes to women and power.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying what the Bassae Frieze depicts (an Amazonomachy — Greeks fighting Amazons, carved in marble, originally in the Temple of Apollo at Bassae). 1 mark for explaining the symbolism (the Amazons represent disorder and the inversion of natural gender roles; Greeks defeating them symbolises civilised order). 1 mark for connecting to broader Greek culture (the Amazonomachy was repeated on the Parthenon metopes, showing how widespread this symbolic narrative was). 1 mark for a more critical point (the repeated need to show Greeks defeating Amazons suggests the threat they represented was not dismissed lightly; or, the fact that Amazons are given heroic qualities in the carving suggests ambivalence, not simple contempt).

practice_questions.text: How similar are the Greek and Roman approaches to the warrior woman? Refer to both literary and visual sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A well-structured comparative essay using literary sources (Virgil's Aeneid Book 11 on Camilla; knowledge of Penthesilea's story from vase painting tradition) and visual/material sources (Bassae Frieze; Parthenon Amazonomachy metopes). Identifies genuine similarities: in both cultures the warrior woman is admired for her courage and fighting skill; in both, she is ultimately defeated by a male hero; in both, her death can be read as restoring conventional gender order. Identifies real differences: Greek Amazonomachy tends to be triumphalist and civic (public temple decoration designed to celebrate Greek victory); Virgil's Camilla is more nuanced and elegiac, and he mourns her death. Notes that both traditions use the warrior woman to explore what female capability and freedom would look like — and then contain it. Reaches a supported, nuanced judgement.
Secure: Makes a clear comparison with named examples from both cultures and at least one source type. Identifies both similarities and differences. Reaches a conclusion.
Developing: Covers both cultures but the comparison is uneven; may focus mainly on one figure or not distinguish clearly between literary and material sources.
Emerging: Covers one culture or makes only general observations without using named sources consistently.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which the representation of warrior women in ancient art reveals cultural attitudes about gender.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: warrior women are always depicted as ultimately defeated (suggesting battle is a male sphere); the battles are placed on public temples (showing these attitudes were civic, not just personal); Amazons are portrayed as foreign or mythological (distancing the threat from real Greek women); the beauty of Amazon figures in sculpture suggests admiration alongside fear; the Amazonomachy appears alongside the Centauromachy (equating women warriors with half-human monsters as both forms of disorder).

before.content_html:
The Problem of the Sources

Every ancient text we have on women was written by a man. In Athens and Rome, literacy was predominantly a male achievement; writing history, biography, comedy, and philosophy was an activity performed almost entirely by men of the educated classes. This is not a trivial problem: it means that every portrait of a real woman that survives — praising Cornelia as the ideal mother, condemning Clodia as immoral, sympathising with Neaira as a victim — is filtered through a male perspective that had its own values, anxieties, and purposes. Understanding the bias in a source is not the same as dismissing it; a biased source still tells us things, but we must ask what it is actually evidence for.

Cornelia: the Ideal Roman Mother

Cornelia, daughter of the great general Scipio Africanus and mother of the Gracchi brothers (the reforming tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus), was one of the most celebrated women in Roman tradition. After her husband’s death, she refused a second marriage — even, allegedly, a proposal from the Egyptian king Ptolemy VIII — and devoted herself to her children’s education. A famous story, told by the ancient author Valerius Maximus and repeated by others, describes a visitor showing off her jewellery, and Cornelia gesturing to her children: “These are my jewels.” Whether this happened or not, the anecdote perfectly encapsulates what Roman culture wanted a great woman to be: a mother whose only ornament was her sons’ excellence.

Cornelia was also known in antiquity for her education. The Roman author and lawyer Cicero praised the quality of her Latin style in a collection of her letters, though those letters no longer survive. Her reputation for learning is significant: in the Roman world, a woman’s education was generally directed towards making her a better wife and mother. But Cornelia’s intellectual cultivation was taken seriously in its own right, and she was used in Roman culture as proof that high female education was not threatening if it was properly channelled through the maternal role.

Key Fact

Cornelia was the daughter of Scipio Africanus and mother of the reforming tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. The famous story of her pointing to her children as “my jewels” made her the Roman ideal of the devoted, educated mother. She refused a second marriage to focus on her sons’ upbringing.

Lucretia: Virtue, Rape and the Foundation of the Republic

Lucretia is one of the most celebrated figures of Roman legend. According to the tradition recorded by Livy (History of Rome 1.57–59, a prescribed source), Lucretia was the wife of a Roman nobleman and the model of wifely virtue. When the Roman princes were boasting about their wives’ qualities, Lucretia was found spinning wool with her maids at night while other wives were at dinner parties. Her modesty and industry were the proof of her virtue. Her rape by Sextus Tarquinius, the son of Rome’s last king, outraged the Roman nobility. Lucretia called her father and husband, told them what had happened, and stabbed herself, declaring that she would not provide a precedent for unchaste Roman women. Her death triggered the revolt led by Brutus that expelled the Tarquin dynasty and established the Roman Republic.

Livy’s account is a prescribed literary source and should be read carefully. It is written six centuries after the events he describes, and the story of Lucretia serves a clear political purpose in his narrative: to explain the founding of the Republic as a moral as well as political revolution. Lucretia’s importance in Roman culture lay not in her political agency (she died) but in her role as a symbol of what Roman virtue was and why Rome’s monarchy was intolerable. Her suicide is presented not as defeat but as an act of supreme moral courage that forced Rome’s men to act. Modern readers often note, however, that the story ultimately places the burden of maintaining sexual virtue on the woman, not the man who raped her.

Hetairai (singular: hetaira) were women who maintained long-term relationships with men outside of marriage — educated companions who attended symposia (drinking parties), were expected to be witty and musically accomplished, and who occupied an ambiguous social position. They were not citizens; they had no kyrios (male guardian) in the conventional sense; they were both admired and condemned. The most famous was Aspasia of Miletus, companion of Pericles, whom we encountered in the previous lesson. Another figure preserved in the sources is Neaira, whose entire history we know only because she was the subject of a court speech (Against Neaira), attributed to Demosthenes, in which her former partner sought to humiliate her former companion by proving she was a former slave and prostitute who had fraudulently posed as an Athenian citizen. Even this hostile source, designed to ruin her reputation, inadvertently preserves details of Neaira’s life that make her one of the most fully documented ordinary women of the ancient world.

Literary versus Material Sources: What Can Each Tell Us?

Literary sources can be detailed, narrative, and contextual — but they are biased, written by men, and often designed to make a moral or political argument rather than to describe reality. Material sources (sculpture, painted pottery, inscribed stelai, frescoes) were made by men too, but they were produced for different purposes — commemoration, display, religious offering — and they can corroborate or challenge the literary record in valuable ways.

The Hegeso Stele (now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens) is a prescribed visual source. Dating to around 410 BC, it shows a seated woman identified by the inscription as Hegeso, daughter of Proxenos, elegantly dressed and examining a piece of jewellery from a decorated box that a standing slave girl holds out to her. The carving is sensitive and restrained: Hegeso is shown as dignified, leisured, and wealthy. The choice of jewellery as her defining activity connects to the ideals of wifely beauty and adornment, but it also shows a woman with resources and domestic authority. Comparing Hegeso’s stele with the literary portrait of the respectable Athenian wife — confined to the home, managing the household — gives the ideal a face and a presence.

The Ampharete Stele (Kerameikos Museum, Athens) is another prescribed material source. It depicts a woman holding a small baby on her lap, with an inscription that records the speaker’s love for the child: “I hold here the dear child of my daughter, whom I held on my knees while alive and looking on the sunlight; now dead, I hold here the dead.” This inscription (unlike most funerary stelai, which simply name the deceased) gives us a direct expression of grandmother’s grief and love. The material source, combined with its inscription, provides a glimpse of emotional experience that the literary sources rarely offer for real, non-famous women.

Key Fact

The Hegeso Stele (c. 410 BC, National Archaeological Museum, Athens) depicts a seated Athenian woman choosing jewellery from a box held by a slave girl. As a prescribed material source it gives the ideal of the respectable Athenian wife a visual presence, showing her wealth, dignity and domestic authority in a way that literary sources only describe abstractly.

A fresco from Pompeii (now in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples) depicts a young woman holding a set of writing tablets to her lips and a stylus, gazing thoughtfully as if in the process of composing something. The fresco is often called the “Sappho” fresco because of its association with female literary creativity, though the woman depicted is not identified as the Greek poet. As a prescribed visual source it is significant because it shows a woman of clearly high status (fine jewellery, elaborate hair) in the act of literary or intellectual work: she is not weaving, or managing a slave, or adorning herself, but thinking and writing. This challenges a simple picture of Roman women as entirely confined to domestic activities and provides evidence for educated, literate women at Pompeii. The visual source complements the literary evidence of Cornelia’s praised writing style, suggesting that female literacy, while not universal, was valued in the upper classes of both Republican and Imperial Rome.
